Findings/result obtained from an electrocardiogram.
Test that records the electrical activity and rhythm of the heart.

Two-dimensional ultrasound examination of the heart.

Describes the appearance and characteristics of white blood cells.
White blood cells involved in allergic and inflammatory responses.

Percentage of blood volume occupied by red blood cells.

Number of red blood cells in a given volume of blood.

Total number of white blood cells in the blood.

Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration; average concentration of hemoglobin within red blood cells.

Absolute number of neutrophils in the blood.

Absolute number of monocytes in the blood.
Absolute number of basophils in the blood.

Platelet Distribution Width; reflects variation in platelet size.
Standard deviation-based measure of variation in red blood cell size.
Plateletcrit; percentage of blood volume occupied by platelets.
Platelet Large Cell Ratio; proportion of larger platelets in the circulation.
Rh blood-group status, generally reported as positive or negative based on the presence of the Rh(D) antigen.
Identifies the person's ABO blood group: A, B, AB or O.
Time required for blood to form a clot under specified test conditions.
Historical test assessing the time required for bleeding to stop; relates mainly to platelet function and primary hemostasis.
Measures the time required for blood to clot through the extrinsic/common coagulation pathways.
Same coagulation measurement as PT; used to evaluate clotting and commonly monitor warfarin therapy.
Measures vitamin B12 concentration, important for red blood cell formation and normal nervous-system function.
Measures 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the main circulating form used to assess vitamin D status.
Measures glycated blood proteins and provides an estimate of average blood glucose over roughly the previous 2–3 weeks.
Fasting Blood Sugar; blood glucose measured after fasting, commonly used for diabetes screening and monitoring.
Random Blood Sugar; blood glucose measured at any time regardless of when food was last consumed.
Post-Prandial Blood Sugar; blood glucose measured after a meal, commonly around 2 hours after eating.
Glycated hemoglobin; reflects average blood glucose over approximately the previous 2–3 months.
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test; measures the body's response to a standardized glucose load and is used particularly for diagnosing glucose intolerance/diabetes and gestational diabetes.
Ratio of LDL cholesterol to HDL cholesterol; provides a comparative view of these two cholesterol fractions.
Ratio of total cholesterol to HDL cholesterol.
High-Density Lipoprotein cholesterol; commonly called "good cholesterol" because higher levels are generally associated with lower cardiovascular risk.
Very-Low-Density Lipoprotein cholesterol; primarily transports triglycerides in the blood.
Low-Density Lipoprotein cholesterol; elevated levels are associated with increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
Total amount of cholesterol in the blood, including cholesterol carried by different lipoproteins.
A major type of fat in the blood; elevated levels can contribute to cardiovascular and metabolic risk.
Main structural protein of atherogenic lipoprotein particles such as LDL, VLDL and remnants; reflects the number of atherogenic particles.
Same marker as Apolipoprotein B; duplicate naming.
Main protein component of HDL particles and involved in reverse cholesterol transport.
LDL-like lipoprotein containing apolipoprotein(a); genetically influenced cardiovascular risk marker.
Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT); enzyme associated particularly with the liver and biliary system.
Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT); liver enzyme that can increase when liver cells are damaged.
Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST); enzyme found in liver, heart and muscles that may increase with tissue injury.
Enzyme associated with liver/bile ducts and bone; elevated levels can occur in several liver or bone conditions.
Total bilirubin in blood, reflecting breakdown of hemoglobin and processing/excretion by the liver.
Conjugated bilirubin processed by the liver and generally excreted through bile.
Unconjugated bilirubin formed before liver conjugation.
General measurement of bilirubin; may refer to total or a specific fraction depending on the report.
Major protein produced by the liver; helps maintain fluid balance and transports various substances.
Group of blood proteins involved in immune function and transport.
Total amount of major proteins in blood, generally including albumin and globulins.
Albumin-to-Globulin ratio; compares two major groups of blood proteins.
Measures small amounts of albumin in urine; useful for detecting early kidney damage, particularly in diabetes.
Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate; estimates how effectively the kidneys filter blood.
Measures urea in blood, a waste product produced from protein metabolism and eliminated by the kidneys.
Blood Urea Nitrogen; measures the nitrogen component of urea in blood.
Waste product produced mainly by muscle metabolism and filtered by the kidneys; commonly used to assess kidney function.
Estimates the kidney's ability to clear creatinine from the blood.
Measures creatinine concentration in urine; used in kidney assessment and for interpreting urine protein/albumin measurements.
Ratio between BUN and creatinine; can help interpret patterns of kidney function and hydration.
Ratio of urea to creatinine, used to assess the relationship between these kidney-related markers.
Estimates urinary protein excretion while accounting for urine concentration.
Same concept as urine protein-to-creatinine ratio; estimates protein loss in urine.
Measures albumin excreted into urine and can indicate kidney damage when elevated.
Electrolyte involved in fluid balance, acid-base regulation and maintenance of electrical neutrality.
Mineral important for bones, energy metabolism and cellular function.
Mineral essential for bones, muscles, nerves and blood clotting.
Major electrolyte involved in fluid balance, nerve function and muscle function.
Major intracellular electrolyte essential for nerve signaling and normal heart and muscle function.
Urine pH indicates how acidic or alkaline the urine is.
Unbound triiodothyronine available to tissues; an active thyroid hormone.
Total triiodothyronine, a thyroid hormone involved in regulating metabolism.
Total thyroxine, the primary hormone produced by the thyroid gland.
Unbound thyroxine available to tissues; commonly used with TSH to assess thyroid function.
Hormone produced by the pituitary gland that regulates thyroid hormone production.
Unsaturated Iron-Binding Capacity; measures the amount of transferrin available to bind additional iron.
Likely a system-specific variation/code for UIBC; underlying parameter measures unsaturated iron-binding capacity.
Likely a system-specific variation/code for UIBC; measures unsaturated iron-binding capacity.
Estimates the blood's capacity to bind iron, mainly through transferrin.
Measures iron concentration in blood, generally reflecting circulating serum iron.
Percentage of transferrin binding sites occupied by iron; helps assess iron availability and iron disorders.
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein; detects relatively low levels of inflammation and is commonly used in cardiovascular risk assessment.
Protein produced in response to inflammation; a nonspecific marker of inflammatory activity.
Autoantibody that can be present in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune/infectious conditions.
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody; relatively specific autoimmune marker associated with rheumatoid arthritis.
Enzyme involved in carbohydrate digestion; mainly produced by the pancreas and salivary glands.
Enzyme primarily produced by the pancreas that helps digest dietary fats; commonly assessed in suspected pancreatic disease.
Also called creatine kinase (CK); enzyme found in skeletal muscle, heart and brain that can rise with muscle injury.
Waste product formed from purine metabolism; elevated levels can contribute to gout and may be associated with kidney/metabolic conditions.
Indicates bacteria detected in urine; interpretation depends on quantity and other findings because contamination is possible.
Indicates urine concentration and provides information about hydration and the kidney's concentrating ability.
Microscopic crystals in urine; certain types may be associated with kidney stones or metabolic conditions.
Red blood cells detected in urine; may indicate blood in the urine.
Bilirubin-related pigments detected in urine; may be associated with certain liver or biliary conditions.
Protein detected in urine; persistent elevation may indicate kidney disease.
Indicates blood/hemoglobin detected in urine.
Glucose detected in urine; may occur when blood glucose is sufficiently elevated or in certain renal conditions.
Fungal/yeast cells detected in urine; may indicate contamination or urinary fungal involvement depending on context.
Non-specific microscopic material/crystals found in urine sediment.
Urine marker that can become positive when certain bacteria convert nitrate to nitrite; may support a urinary tract infection.
Visual description of urine, such as clear, cloudy or turbid.
Parasite that can cause trichomoniasis; detection in a urine/genital specimen can indicate infection.
Bile-related substances detected in urine; may be associated with liver or biliary disease.
Cylindrical structures formed in kidney tubules; different types can provide clues about kidney conditions.
Produced when the body breaks down fat for energy; can increase with fasting, low-carbohydrate diets or uncontrolled diabetes.
Product formed from bilirubin metabolism; urine levels can provide information about liver function and red-cell breakdown.
White blood cells in urine; can indicate urinary inflammation or infection.
Amount/volume of urine specimen or another specimen-related measurement; not a biomarker itself.
Visual color of urine; affected by hydration, foods, medications and disease.

Forced Vital Capacity measured after bronchodilator administration.

Forced Vital Capacity measured before bronchodilator administration.
Amount of air remaining in the lungs after maximum forced exhalation.
Group of tests assessing lung volumes, airflow and respiratory capacity.
Measurement/observation related to the process of breathing air out.
Overall clinical interpretation of the pulmonary test.
FEV1 measured after bronchodilator administration.
Peak Expiratory Flow measured before bronchodilator; maximum speed of forced expiration.
Measurement/observation related to breathing air into the lungs.
FEV1-to-FVC ratio after bronchodilator administration.
Peak Expiratory Flow after bronchodilator administration.
Forced Vital Capacity; maximum amount of air that can be forcefully exhaled after a full inhalation.
Forced Expiratory Volume in one second; amount of air exhaled during the first second of a forceful breath.
Peak Expiratory Flow Rate; maximum speed at which air can be forcefully exhaled.
Antibodies against Hepatitis C virus; indicates exposure to HCV but does not by itself confirm active infection.
Hepatitis B e-antigen; marker associated with active HBV replication/infectivity in appropriate clinical contexts.
Detects/measures Hepatitis B viral genetic material and can indicate active viral replication.
Hepatitis B surface antigen; indicates current Hepatitis B infection when confirmed appropriately.
HIV screening/detection test; exact meaning depends on the assay used.
Test specifically assessing HIV-2 infection/antibodies or antigen depending on the assay.
Blood marker commonly used in monitoring certain ovarian cancers; can also be elevated in several non-cancerous conditions.
Prostate-Specific Antigen; protein produced by prostate tissue and used primarily in prostate health assessment and cancer screening/monitoring.
Imaging report of breast tissue used primarily for breast cancer screening and evaluation of breast abnormalities.
Cervical cell examination used to screen for cervical precancerous changes and cancer.
Consultation with a gynecologist; not a biomarker.
X-ray imaging of the chest used to assess lungs, heart size and other thoracic structures.
Posteroanterior chest X-ray view, commonly used for chest/lung assessment.
Computed tomography imaging that produces detailed cross-sectional images of the body.
Panoramic dental X-ray providing a broad view of the teeth, jaws and surrounding structures.
Likely Doppler ultrasound; evaluates blood flow through vessels using ultrasound.
CT angiography; CT imaging performed with contrast to visualize blood vessels.
Imaging using high-frequency sound waves to visualize internal structures.
Ultrasound examination of kidneys and urinary system.
Ultrasound examination of abdominal organs.
Same as whole-abdomen ultrasound.
Imaging using X-rays to visualize internal structures, particularly bones and certain organs.
X-ray of the kidneys, ureters and bladder.
